gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 16-inch 2560x1600 120 Hz screen that sits above the MacBook (Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro) runs in a Limited Power Mode on the laptop's cable alone, drawing 7.5 W with brightness capped at 80%, and needs a USB-C PD charger of 15 W or more for full brightness; nor that the 65 W it passes back is under half of the 140 W adapter Apple ships with the 16-inch MacBook Pro.
standout_why: Compared against the cited Macworld roundup, PCWorld roundup, RTINGS and TechRadar (the last two only partly rendered; seattlepi could not be fetched). Macworld's roundup lists the Float 2 Pro with '65W pass-through charging' but gives no watt figure for port output or monitor draw, no brightness cap on one cable, and never mentions the 140 W charger. PCWorld only recommends a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alt Mode and Power Delivery. The 7.5 W / 80% / 15 W figures exist only in Macworld's separate Float 2 Pro review (Simon Jary, Dec 16 2025), which was not among ChatGPT's results, so the finding is new to the answer but a rival publisher has part of it elsewhere. I held it at 2 because it qualifies the pick rather than overturning it.
decides: It confirms the Duex Float 2 Pro as a workable one-cable pick on a 16-inch MacBook Pro, with two conditions the page must state. First, its 350-nit figure applies with a PD charger of 15 W or more plugged into the screen; on the Mac's cable alone Macworld reports 7.5 W draw and an 80% brightness cap. Second, a wall charger through the screen passes back up to 65 W, against Apple's 140 W adapter, and none of Apple's listed fast-charge setups for the 16-inch is that low, so a shopper who works plugged in should keep MagSafe on the Mac. The brightness ranking between the Float 2 Pro (350 nits) and the UPERFECT GR16DQ (400 nits per the desk lead) should therefore say which power condition each figure assumes; I could not source the UPERFECT's draw or any cap.

findings.label: Power draw and brightness cap on the laptop's cable alone
findings.value: 7.5 W in Limited Power Mode, brightness capped at 80%
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro review: Portable screen that floats above your MacBook (Macworld, Simon Jary, Dec 16 2025)
findings.note: Macworld (Simon Jary): 'The screen will draw from 7.5W of power from the MacBook in the Limited Power Mode that caps brightness at 80%.' The review does not name the MacBook used for this; an M2 MacBook Pro is mentioned only for a speaker comparison.

findings.label: What full brightness needs
findings.value: A PD-compliant USB-C charger rated 15 W or higher connected to the screen
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary)
findings.note: Macworld (Simon Jary): 'To achieve full brightness and prevent flickering, you can connect a PD-compliant USB-C charger rated at 15W or higher.'

findings.label: Pass-through charging to the laptop
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary)
findings.note: Macworld (Simon Jary): 'When connected to a wall charger the screen can pass-back up to 65W to the connected laptop.' Also: 'The Duex Float 2 displays don't include a built-in battery.' Arithmetic: 65 / 140 = 46% of the wattage of Apple's included adapter.

findings.label: Panel and weight as Macworld reports them
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary)
findings.note: Macworld (Simon Jary): 'Maximum brightness is 350 nits, with a 1200:1 contrast ratio and a 120Hz refresh rate'; 'the whole thing weighs in at 2.9lbs (1.3kg)'; 'The Duex Float 2 Pro mirrors the 16-inch display of the top-end MacBook Pro.' The review says nothing about 120 Hz behaviour on a Mac. Pixel-density arithmetic: sqrt(2560^2 + 1600^2) / 16 = 188.7 ppi.

findings.label: Store price today
findings.source_title: Duex Float 2 Pro (Mobile Pixels US store)
findings.note: Read with storecheck.py (search and product). The product URL slug is /products/duex-float; variant id 42255313141826. The page itself returned HTTP 429 to a direct fetch twice, so no spec text was read from it.

findings.label: Power a Thunderbolt 4 computer port supplies to a bus-powered accessory
findings.note: Intel: 'Quick charging: Up to 100W of power for laptop charging and up to 15W for computer-powered accessories.' This applies to the 2021 and 2023 16-inch MacBook Pro models, which I recall having Thunderbolt 4 ports but did not check today; the 2024 model has Thunderbolt 5 (Apple spec page), for which I did not source a figure.

findings.label: 16-inch MacBook Pro (2024) battery, adapter and ports
findings.value: 100 Wh battery (99.6 Wh actual per footnote); 140W USB-C Power Adapter; three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports supporting charging and DisplayPort
findings.note: Apple: 'Fast-charge capable with included 140W USB-C Power Adapter.' Arithmetic: a 7.5 W screen draw is 7.5% of a 100 Wh battery per hour, on top of the Mac's own use. This is the 2024 model's page; I did not open a page for a later model.

findings.label: 16-inch MacBook Pro (2024) built-in display and external display support
findings.value: 16.2-inch, 3456 x 2234 at 254 ppi, ProMotion up to 120 Hz; M4 Pro drives up to two external displays at up to 6K 60 Hz over Thunderbolt
findings.note: Apple: '3456-by-2234 native resolution at 254 pixels per inch'; 'ProMotion technology for adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz'. A 16-inch 2560 x 1600 panel is 188.7 ppi by arithmetic, about 74% of the MacBook's density, so text is less sharp than on the built-in screen.

findings.label: Apple's fast-charge setups for the 16-inch MacBook Pro
findings.value: 140W adapter + USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable; 140W adapter + 240W USB-C Charge Cable (Nov 2023 model or later); Apple Studio Display XDR + Thunderbolt cable
findings.source_title: Fast-charge your MacBook Air or MacBook Pro (Apple Support, published November 05, 2026)
findings.note: Section '16-inch MacBook Pro (2021 or later)'. No 65 W source is listed, and the page does not say what happens on a lower-wattage source.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Duex Float (original model, not the Float 2 Pro)
findings.label: Maker's own statement of the same bus-power pattern on the earlier model
findings.value: 250 nits when powered from the computer, up to 300 nits with external power; 'Max at 7W'
findings.note: Mobile Pixels: 'The max brightness of the Duex Float is by default set at 250 nits when is directly powered of a computer... if a proper external power is supplied to the Duex Float, the max brightness can go up to 300 nits.' The FAQ covers only the original Duex Float; use as context, not as a Float 2 Pro spec. It also says plug-and-play needs 'a USB-C port with DisplayPort enabled'.

findings.label: What the cited Macworld roundup says about the Float 2 Pro and power
findings.value: Lists it as 16-inch 2560 x 1600 at 120 Hz with '65W pass-through charging', price when reviewed $299.99; no watt figures for port output or monitor draw; 140 W charger not mentioned
findings.note: The roundup also says plain M1 and M2 Macs 'are limited to connecting just a single monitor' and that the Trio 3 Pro 'will need to download and install free software (rather like DisplayLink)'. It has nothing on macOS scaling or on a brightness cap on one cable.

findings.label: What the cited PCWorld roundup says about the connection
findings.value: Recommends a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alternate Mode and USB Power Delivery; no monitor power draw stated
findings.source_title: Best portable monitors 2026: Displays that go with you (PCWorld)
findings.note: PCWorld: 'We recommend buying a portable monitor that has a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alternate Mode and USB Power Delivery.' No 16-inch 2560 x 1600 120 Hz model appears in what was rendered.

Whether a MacBook Pro port on its own lifts the Float 2 Pro out of Limited Power Mode, and the Float 2 Pro's draw at 100% brightness and 120 Hz. Macworld gives only the 7.5 W limited-mode figure.

Mobile Pixels' own product-page statements for the Float 2 Pro (fit range, 65 W pass-through, 350 nits, USB-C requirement). The page returned HTTP 429 twice; storecheck returned only price, stock and a one-line tagline.

Power draw, any low-power brightness cap, and which input carries 120 Hz for the UPERFECT GR16DQ, Arzopa Z1RC, ASUS ZenScreen MB16QHG and Mobile Pixels Fold 16 QHD. None of their pages or manuals were read for this angle.

Apple's wording on choosing 120 Hz for an external display, and on scaled 'looks like' resolutions on a non-Retina-density panel. No Apple page was opened for either; the 188.7 ppi against 254 ppi comparison is arithmetic from stated resolutions.
Apple's statement of what happens when a 16-inch MacBook Pro is fed by a source under 140 W, such as 65 W. The fast-charge page does not address it and search surfaced only community-forum answers.
The seattlepi.com cited page could not be fetched. The RTINGS and TechRadar pages rendered without their product lists, so their coverage of this point is unchecked beyond the visible text.
